verdict: Caution: lend selectively to bidi/tobacco trade and processing units with clean GST and tight stock limits; avoid cigarette-dependent retail and any unit with tax-hit margin stress.
title: Nizamabad Tobacco Products & Bidi: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Bidi and tobacco products in Nizamabad are a labour-and-leaf business, not a factory business.** A unit buys tendu leaf and tobacco, pays rolling hands by the thousand sticks, and sells through distributors and wholesale channels. Cash sits in finished-stock and distributor credit, not in machines. **So when a proposal lands, check the leaf-to-stick conversion cost and the distributor credit days first; if the borrower cannot show both, ask for the stock register and the last six months of GST returns.**

## What has changed now
**The national signal is negative: IIP for NIC 12 output is -8.0% YoY and -4.4% Apr-to-date [D].** Peer Godfrey Phillips reported Q1FY27 net profit down 44%, revenue down 18.9% to Rs 1,205.5 crore from Rs 1,486.2 crore, on higher tobacco taxation and lower cigarette volumes [4][5]. Management said it is phasing price increases to consumers [6]. **That is a margin-compression story, and it reaches Nizamabad through distributor credit and stock value.** Telangana itself is running hot — GST collections +13.8% Apr-to-date vs India +6.1%, electricity demand +15.7% vs India +9.5% [D] — but that is a broad state tailwind, not a tobacco-specific one. **Local sources say almost nothing about Nizamabad tobacco; the only local item is a dispute over cigarettes that ended in a self-immolation [1], which tells us enforcement and price friction are live, not that demand is growing.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue the leaf-and-rolling units and the wholesale distributors who sell across categories, not the single-cigarette retail counter.** The migrant-labour sowing activity around Nizamabad [2] points to a working agricultural base that supports trade credit. **Take the bidi units with own rolling sheds and repeat distributor relationships; avoid pure cigarette-retail borrowers whose entire margin depends on one brand's price ladder.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure as cash-flow lending against stock and receivables, not against fixed assets.** Take monthly GST returns, stock statements and distributor ageing every month; a bidi unit's real collateral is its turnover cycle. **Set a covenant that stock days and distributor credit days cannot both rise in the same quarter; if they do, ask for the reason in writing before renewing.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for falling volumes with flat prices — that is the Godfrey Phillips pattern [3][5] arriving at a small unit.** Also watch brand piracy, which ICRA flagged as a volume drag on a bidi manufacturer [9]. **If a borrower's GST turnover falls two months running while stock rises, cut the limit.**
watch: two consecutive months of falling turnover with rising stock -> freeze enhancement, review limit
stock days and credit days both up in one quarter -> ask for written reason, hold renewal
further negative YoY print -> tighten new-to-bank tobacco exposure
another peer profit fall on tax -> reprice or reduce cigarette-linked retail lines
